terms.definition: one input column, seen as one direction in space: a table with 784 columns is a 784-dimensional dataset, and each row is a point in that space.
the number of dimensions (columns) a dataset has.
the book's name for everything that goes wrong when a dataset has very many columns: training slows down and good solutions get harder to find.
turning a table with many columns into one with fewer columns while keeping as much of the useful information as possible.
a famous dataset of 70,000 small photos of handwritten digits 0 to 9, each 28 × 28 = 784 pixels; the book uses the first 60,000 for training.
one dot of an image, stored as one number (for MNIST: 0 = white, 255 = full black).
drawing the data as a picture (a chart) so a person can see patterns in it.
the box where every coordinate runs from 0 to 1: a unit square in 2 dimensions, a unit cube in 3, a hypercube in more.
a 4-dimensional cube (Figure 8-1's last drawing).
spread thin: the instances are far apart, with lots of empty space between them.
predicting for a point far from every training example, instead of between examples you do have (interpolating).
growing by multiplying, not by adding: each extra step multiplies the total (for example doubles it), so it explodes quickly.
a model that predicts a category (here: which digit an image shows) — the classification version of a regressor.

exclude: \bprojects? onto a hyperplane that keeps classes\b
terms.definition: moving each point straight onto a flat surface (a line or a plane) and reading its position there — like a shadow.
a flat slice of the full space that passes through its centre: a line inside a plane, or a plane inside 3D space.
a toy dataset of points on a flat sheet that has been rolled up in 3D, like a Swiss-roll cake.
a surface that looks flat when you zoom in close, even though it may be bent or rolled up overall (the Swiss roll is a 2D manifold bent into 3D).
the flat surface one dimension smaller than the space it sits in: a line in 2D, a plane in 3D, and so on.
reducing dimensions by modelling the bent surface the data lies on and unrolling it, instead of flattening it onto a plane.
the assumption that most real high-dimensional data lies near a much lower-dimensional manifold.
the line or surface a classifier draws between two classes: on one side it predicts one class, on the other side the other.
reducing columns by keeping some of the original columns and deleting the rest.
reducing columns by computing new columns out of all the old ones (what projection does).
how easily a person can say what a column or a model's answer means.
principal component analysis: the most popular dimensionality-reduction algorithm; it finds the directions along which the data is most spread out and projects onto the first few.
one of the directions PCA finds, written as a unit vector. The first keeps the most variance, the second the most of what is left, and so on.
a direction in space: the original x, y, z axes are the dataset's columns; PCA's new axes are directions it picks through the data.
at right angles to each other; two orthogonal directions share nothing, so one says nothing about the other.
an arrow of length exactly 1 that only says "this direction".
the point where every coordinate is 0.
a rule of thumb that usually works but is not guaranteed.
linear discriminant analysis: a classification algorithm whose learned directions keep the classes as far apart as possible; it can also be used to reduce dimensions.
a grid of numbers, rows by columns — the maths name for a NumPy array with two dimensions.
singular value decomposition: a standard recipe that splits any matrix X into three matrices U, Σ and V transpose; for PCA, V holds the principal components.
rewriting one object as a product of simpler ones, the way 12 can be written as 3 × 4.
a matrix flipped over its diagonal, so its rows become columns (written with a raised T).
the maths of vectors and matrices (adding them, multiplying them).
subtracting each column's average from every value in it, so each column's new average is 0 and the cloud of points sits around the origin.
the list s that SVD returns, largest first: how much the data is stretched along each principal component.
the row-by-column arithmetic behind `@` in NumPy: multiply matching entries of a row and a column and add them up, for every row-column pair.
for one principal component: the share of the data's total variance that lies along it (0.758 means 75.8%).
a running total: entry i is the sum of the first i+1 values (np.cumsum).
the bend in a curve where it stops rising (or falling) steeply and flattens out.
the POSITION of the largest value in an array (not the value itself); np.argmax.
for a classifier: the share of instances it labels correctly (0.858 = 85.8%).
Scikit-Learn's linear classifier trained by stochastic gradient descent (a gradient method that learns from one small random sample of rows at a time).
storing data with fewer numbers; decompression rebuilds (an approximation of) the original.
how much a compress-then-decompress round trip loses: the average squared distance between each original point and its rebuilt copy.
running a transformation backwards: here, mapping the reduced data back to the original number of columns (inverse_transform).
compression that throws some information away for good (JPEG is lossy; zip is not).
a faster version of PCA that uses random sampling to find only the first d components approximately, instead of computing all of them exactly.
using randomness inside the algorithm, so the result can differ a little from run to run.
a version of PCA that learns from the data one chunk (mini-batch) at a time with partial_fit(), so the whole dataset never has to be in memory.
a small chunk of rows processed in one step, instead of the whole dataset at once.
the Scikit-Learn method that continues learning from one more chunk of data, keeping what was learned from earlier chunks (fit would start over).
a NumPy array stored in a file on disk that your code uses like a normal in-memory array; only the pieces you touch are loaded.
shorthand for how cost grows: O(n²) means doubling n makes the work about four times bigger.
reducing dimensions by multiplying the data by a matrix of random numbers — nothing is learned from the data.
a maths result: a random projection to enough dimensions keeps the distances between points almost unchanged, with high probability; it also gives the minimum number of dimensions.
a proven maths statement (a small theorem).
the Greek letter ε; here, the tolerance: how much a squared distance may change (0.1 = 10%).
the distance between two points, for every pair of points in the data.
the best available stand-in for undoing a matrix multiplication when the matrix is not square and has no true inverse.
how full something is: for data, how many points sit in a region of the space; for a table of numbers (b09), the share of its cells that are not zero.
locally linear embedding: a manifold-learning algorithm that describes each point by its nearest neighbours, then finds new low-dimensional positions that keep those same descriptions.
a number that says how much one input counts when things are multiplied and added up; a bigger weight means that input matters more.
all the LLE weights in one table: one row per point, one column per point, zero everywhere except each point's k neighbours.
the new low-dimensional positions an algorithm gives to the points.
"the value that makes this smallest" (np.argmin returns its position).
a limit or rule that must be respected: a memory or time limit, or (b10) a rule the weights must obey.
growing with the square: 10 times the rows means 100 times the work.
multidimensional scaling: reduces dimensions while trying to keep the straight-line distance between every pair of points.
reduces dimensions while keeping distances measured ALONG the data's surface (through a graph of neighbours), not straight through space.
distance measured along a surface (or along a graph's links), not in a straight line through the air.
points (called nodes) joined by links; here each point is linked to its nearest neighbours.
t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding: reduces dimensions (usually to 2) keeping similar points together and pushing different ones apart; used to look at clusters.
a square table with one row and one column per input column, holding how strongly every pair of columns varies together (the diagonal holds each column's variance).
the Python library for drawing charts (plt.plot, plt.scatter, plt.imshow).
running one reduction after another: a fast one to remove most columns, then a slow one on what is left.
